claim: The Mediator complex stimulates the cooperative assembly of a pre-initiation complex (PIC) and recruitment of RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) for gene activation.
source: The Mediator complex stimulates the cooperative assembly of a pre-initiation complex (PIC) and recruitment of RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) for gene activation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about Mediator function, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: In budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), the core Mediator complex is organized into head, middle, and tail modules.
source: In budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), Mediator is composed of 25 subunits divided into four domains based on structural and functional criteria: the tail, middle, head, and kinase modules (Guglielmi et al., 2004; Plaschka et al., 2016; van de Peppel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural and functional studies.

claim: Mediator recruitment in yeast has generally been ascribed to sequence-specific activators engaging the tail module triad of Med2-Med3-Med15 at upstream activating sequences (UASs).
source: Mediator recruitment has generally been ascribed to sequence-specific activators engaging the tail module triad of Med2-Med3-Med15 (Lee et al., 1999; Myers et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2004; Ansari and Morse, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Yeast lacking Med2-Med3-Med15 are viable.
source: We show that yeast lacking Med2-Med3-Med15 are viable
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, demonstrated experimentally.

claim: Mediator and Pol II are recruited to promoters genome-wide in med2Δ med3Δ med15Δ cells, albeit at reduced levels.
source: We show that yeast lacking Med2-Med3-Med15 are viable and that Mediator and PolII are recruited to promoters genome-wide in these cells, albeit at reduced levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Depletion of Taf1, Rpb3, and TBP profoundly affected Mediator association at active gene promoters.
source: We found that depletion of Taf1, Rpb3, and TBP profoundly affected Mediator association at active gene promoters
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-seq experiments after anchor away depletion.

claim: TBP is critical for transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter.
source: with TBP being critical for transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-seq data showing upstream shift of Mediator upon TBP depletion.

claim: Pol II and Taf1 stabilize Mediator association at proximal promoters.
source: while Pol II and Taf1 stabilize Mediator association at proximal promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP-seq data showing reduced Mediator occupancy upon depletion of these factors.

claim: The tail module can under some circumstances be recruited independently of the remainder of Mediator.
source: consistent with this model, the tail module can under some circumstances be recruited independently of the remainder of Mediator (Ansari et al., 2009; He et al., 2008; Paul et al., 2015; Petrenko et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2004; Anandhakumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The tail is recruited as a complex with the head, middle, and kinase modules at upstream activating sequences (UASs).
source: Normally, however, the tail is recruited as a complex with the head, middle, and kinase modules at upstream activating sequences (UASs) (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014; Grünberg et al., 2016; Kuras et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once Mediator is recruited, the kinase module dissociates from the complex.
source: Once Mediator is recruited, the kinase module dissociates from the complex and Mediator bridges the enhancer to connect with Pol II and general transcription factors (GTFs) at the proximal promoter of active genes (Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mediator association with the PIC at proximal promoters is quickly disrupted following phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by Kin28.
source: Mediator association with the PIC at proximal promoters is quickly disrupted following phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by Kin28, marking the end of initiation (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Loss of Mediator function results in greatly decreased mRNA levels and concomitant diminished association of Pol II with essentially all Pol II transcribed genes.
source: This orchestrated recruitment of Mediator is broadly required for transcription, evidenced by studies that showed a loss of Mediator function results in greatly decreased mRNA levels and concomitant diminished association of Pol II with essentially all Pol II transcribed genes (Ansari et al., 2009; Holstege et al., 1998; Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Paul et al., 2015; Plaschka et al., 2015; Thompson and Young, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: med3Δ med15Δ yeast are viable.
source: In spite of the purported role of the tail module triad in Mediator recruitment by transcriptional activators, med3Δ med15Δ yeast are viable
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: med3Δ med15Δ yeast show defects in mRNA levels for only 5–10% of active genes during normal growth.
source: med3Δ med15Δ yeast are viable, show defects in mRNA levels for only 5–10% of active genes during normal growth, and exhibit continued Mediator and Pol II occupancy by ChIP-seq (Ansari et al., 2012a; Jeronimo et al., 2016; Paul et al., 2015; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The tail module is not required for Mediator's interaction with the PIC.
source: Additional studies report that the tail module is not required for Mediator's interaction with the PIC (Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016; Plaschka et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Indirect recruitment of Mediator via interactions with the general transcription machinery has been proposed on the basis of in vitro experiments.
source: Indirect recruitment of Mediator via interactions with the general transcription machinery has also been proposed on the basis of in vitro experiments (Johnson and Carey, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior in vitro work.

claim: Loss of Mediator leads to a decrease in PIC components and diminished Pol II presence at active genes.
source: Several studies show that a loss of Mediator leads to a decrease in PIC components and diminished Pol II presence at active genes, highlighting the unilateral importance of Mediator in stimulating the assembly of a PIC (Eyboulet et al., 2015; He et al., 2008; Holstege et al., 1998; Paul et al., 2015; Thompson and Young, 1995; Kuras and Struhl, 1999; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The TFIID-TBP complex and Pol II occupy proximal promoters and have the potential to engage Mediator directly.
source: The TFIID-TBP complex and Pol II in particular occupy proximal promoters and have the potential to engage Mediator directly.
evidence: This is an inference based on known structural and functional properties of these complexes.

claim: Mediator association at proximal promoters is transient.
source: In vivo, however, Mediator's interaction with the PIC at proximal promoters is likely brief in light of recent evidence demonstrating that Mediator association at proximal promoters is transient, making interactions with the PIC difficult to assess in living cells (Fan and Struhl, 2009; Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mediator stabilization at proximal promoters occurs in the kin28-AA strain.
source: We confirm Mediator stabilization at proximal promoters in the kin28-AA strain.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study, supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: In med2Δ med3Δ med15Δ yeast, association of Mediator and Pol II is greatly reduced but nonetheless still detected at the majority of targets.
source: In the same background, we show that in med2Δ med3Δ med15Δ yeast, which completely lack the tail module triad, association of Mediator and Pol II is greatly reduced but nonetheless still detected at the majority of targets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Segregants from diploid yeast heterozygous for MED2, MED3, and MED15 included viable med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ mutants.
source: Segregants from diploid yeast heterozygous for MED2, MED3, and MED15 (complete ORF deletions) included viable med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ mutants
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ mutants showed modest growth defects similar to those seen for med3∆ med15∆ yeast.
source: which showed modest growth defects similar to those seen for med3∆ med15∆ yeast (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by spot dilution assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two independent med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ segregants exhibited genome-wide expression patterns more similar to each other than to wild type yeast.
source: RNA-seq showed that two independent segregants exhibited genome-wide expression patterns more similar to each other than to wild type yeast (Figure 1B) (Fisher's z-score = 37, p<10−10 for the null hypothesis that the correlations are not significantly different).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by RNA-seq data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Down-regulated genes in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast were enriched for SAGA-dominated promoters.
source: Down-regulated genes were enriched for SAGA-dominated promoters (75 of 164 genes down-regulated by >2X in both segregants; p<10−34, hypergeometric test)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by RNA-seq data and statistical analysis.

claim: Up-regulated genes in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast showed marginal enrichment for SAGA-dominated promoters.
source: while up-regulated genes showed marginal enrichment for SAGA-dominated promoters (35 of 442 genes, p=0.04), consistent with previous findings (Ansari et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by RNA-seq data and statistical analysis, consistent with prior work.

claim: Treatment of kin28-AA yeast with rapamycin allowed detection of myc-tagged Med17 at the majority of promoters.
source: Consistent with previous work, treatment of kin28-AA yeast harboring intact Mediator allowed detection of myc-tagged Med17 at the majority of promoters (Figure 1C–D) (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 1C-D, consistent with prior studies.

claim: In kin28-AA yeast lacking the Mediator tail module triad, Med17 ChIP signal was reduced but still detectable at the same promoters.
source: In kin28-AA yeast lacking the Mediator tail module triad, Med17 ChIP signal was reduced much more than the reduction in Mediator occupancy (less than two-fold) reported for med3∆ med15∆ yeast (Jeronimo et al., 2016). Nonetheless, Med17 occupancy was still detectable at the same promoters
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: The reduction in Med17 occupancy in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast was proportionally larger at SAGA-dominated genes than at TFIID-dominated genes.
source: The reduction in Med17 occupancy was proportionally larger at SAGA-dominated genes than at TFIID-dominated genes, possibly reflecting the enrichment of SAGA-dominated genes among genes depending most strongly on the tail module triad for transcription, but association with both categories of gene promoters was generally reduced (Figure 1C–D) (Ansari et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 1C-D.

claim: Mediator occupancy at UAS regions appears to be reduced to near baseline levels in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast.
source: This occupancy appears to be reduced to near baseline levels in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast, as was reported previously for med3∆ med15∆ yeast (Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by ChIP-seq data, consistent with prior studies.

claim: An approximately four-fold decrease in Pol II occupancy was observed in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast.
source: We observed an approximately four-fold decrease in Pol II occupancy in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast, while the normalized spike-in control showed equal IP efficiency in the two samples (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by spike-in normalized ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both Mediator and Pol II occupancy are reduced at essentially all genes in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast.
source: Two features of this data are notable: first, both Mediator and Pol II occupancy are reduced at essentially all genes in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Substantial occupancy by Mediator and Pol II is observed even in the complete absence of the tail module triad.
source: and second, substantial occupancy by Mediator and Pol II is observed even in the complete absence of the tail module triad.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: The tail module triad contributes broadly if not universally to recruitment of Mediator and Pol II, but is not absolutely required at the large majority of mRNA genes.
source: Thus, the tail module triad contributes broadly if not universally to recruitment of Mediator and Pol II, but at the same time is not absolutely required at the large majority of mRNA genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator and Pol II occupancy in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast.

claim: Med15 and Med18 occupancy at UAS regions did not decrease upon depletion of TBP, Rpb3, or Taf1.
source: However, Med15 and Med18 occupancy at UAS regions did not decrease upon depletion of TBP, Rpb3, or Taf1 (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Med15 occupancy at UAS regions was increased relative to that seen before depletion for TBP and Rpb3.
source: For Med15, high occupancy was observed at UAS regions upon depletion of all three PIC components; occupancy was increased relative to that seen before depletion for TBP and Rpb3, but was constitutively high in the taf1-AA strain.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Med15 occupancy increased at UAS sites upon depletion of TBP or Rpb3.
source: This behavior was also evident at individual promoters, as Med15 occupancy increased at UAS sites upon depletion of TBP or Rpb3 but was constitutively high in taf1-AA yeast (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For Med18, the ChIP signal was unchanged by depletion of TBP, Rpb3, or Taf1.
source: For Med18, the ChIP signal was unchanged by depletion of TBP, Rpb3, or Taf1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Depletion of TBP essentially eliminated Pol II association.
source: Depletion of TBP essentially eliminated Pol II association, as expected
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Depletion of Pol II resulted in a moderate reduction in TBP association.
source: while depletion of Pol II resulted in a moderate reduction in TBP association, consistent with recently published work (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D) (Joo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data, consistent with prior work.

claim: Med2 and Med14 showed increased occupancy after depletion of TBP or Rpb3.
source: ChIP-seq before and after depletion of TBP and Rpb3 against another tail module triad subunit, Med2, and against the scaffold subunit Med14 yielded results most similar to those seen with Med15, with both subunits showing increased occupancy after depletion of TBP or Rpb3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Several hundred genes showed increased Mediator occupancy in their UAS regions upon TBP depletion where negligible occupancy was observed under normal growth conditions.
source: Indeed, this analysis revealed several hundred genes that showed increased Mediator occupancy in their UAS regions upon TBP depletion where negligible occupancy was observed by ourselves or others under normal growth conditions (Jeronimo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The 200 genes showing the greatest increase in Med15 occupancy upon TBP depletion revealed a strong enrichment for ribosomal protein (RP) genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the 200 genes from this group showing the greatest increase in Med15 occupancy revealed a strong enrichment for ribosomal protein (RP) genes
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by GO analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Ribosomal protein genes showed increased Mediator occupancy at UAS regions upon depletion of TBP.
source: and a direct examination of RP genes showed increased Mediator occupancy at UAS regions upon depletion of TBP (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: Mediator association with UAS regions does not decrease upon depletion of PIC components.
source: Taken together, the results of Figures 3–4 indicate that Mediator association with UAS regions does not decrease upon depletion of PIC components
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: Mediator association with UAS regions apparently increases upon depletion of TBP or Pol II.
source: and that association apparently increases upon depletion of TBP or Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Depletion of either Taf1 or Rpb3 resulted in decreased occupancy of Med15 and Med18 in comparison to depletion of Kin28 alone at almost all TFIID-dominated genes.
source: Depletion of either Taf1 or Rpb3 resulted in decreased occupancy of Med15 and Med18 in comparison to depletion of Kin28 alone at almost all TFIID-dominated genes (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Decreased Med15 and Med18 occupancy was observed at SAGA-dominated genes and UAS genes upon depletion of Rpb3.
source: Decreased Med15 and Med18 occupancy was also observed at SAGA-dominated genes and UAS genes upon depletion of Rpb3, along with a partial shift towards the UAS region
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Depletion of Taf1 resulted in decreased Med18 occupancy but little change in Med15 occupancy at SAGA-dominated and UAS genes.
source: while depletion of Taf1 also resulted in decreased Med18 occupancy but little change in Med15 occupancy, other than a small upstream shift, at SAGA-dominated and UAS genes.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Under conditions of Kin28 depletion, Mediator occupancy at promoters of TFIID-dominated genes depends on both Taf1 and Pol II.
source: We conclude that under conditions of Kin28 depletion, Mediator occupancy at promoters of TFIID-dominated genes, and to lesser extent SAGA-regulated genes, depends on both Taf1 and Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy after depletion of PIC components.

claim: At SAGA-dominated genes, occupancy of Med15 from the Mediator tail module did not decrease and shifted upstream in kin28-tbp-AA yeast compared to kin28-AA yeast.
source: At SAGA-dominated genes, occupancy of Med15 from the Mediator tail module did not decrease and shifted upstream in kin28-tbp-AA yeast compared to kin28-AA yeast (Figure 5A & C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5A and C.

claim: Depletion of TBP causes Mediator to be stranded at the UAS.
source: The smaller shift seen for TFIID-dominated genes than for SAGA-dominated genes is consistent with the average distance between UAS and TSS being larger for TATA-containing than for TATA-less promoters (Erb and van Nimwegen, 2011; Kristiansson et al., 2009), supporting the notion that depletion of TBP causes Mediator to be stranded at the UAS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and prior knowledge about promoter architecture.

claim: Med18, Med2, and Med17 all showed a shift upstream at SAGA-dominated genes upon TBP depletion, but the signals for these subunits were reduced to varying degrees.
source: Med18, from the head module, as well as Med2 from the tail module triad and Med17 from the head module all showed a shift upstream at SAGA-dominated genes upon TBP depletion, but the signals for these subunits were reduced to varying degrees upon depletion of Kin28 and TBP compared to those observed upon depletion of Kin28 alone (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: At TFIID-dominated genes, depletion of TBP and Kin28 resulted in a nearly complete loss of ChIP signal for Med18, Med2, and Med17.
source: At TFIID-dominated genes, depletion of TBP and Kin28 resulted in a nearly complete loss of ChIP signal for Med18, Med2, and Med17 (Figure 5B and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5B, D and supplementary figures.

claim: Depletion of Rpb3 together with Kin28 strongly decreased occupancy of both Med15 and Med18, especially at TFIID-dominated genes.
source: Depletion of Rpb3 together with Kin28 strongly decreased occupancy of both Med15 and Med18, especially at TFIID-dominated genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A shift in Med15 occupancy to more upstream regions was seen at SAGA-dominated genes upon depletion of Rpb3 and Kin28.
source: In addition, a shift in Med15 occupancy to more upstream regions (together with an overall decrease in occupancy) was seen at SAGA-dominated genes upon depletion of Rpb3 and Kin28 (Figure 5A & C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5A and C.

claim: Depletion of TBP abolishes recruitment of Pol II.
source: Depletion of TBP abolishes recruitment of Pol II (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), and this is also the case when Kin28 is simultaneously depleted (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in supplementary figures and Figure 7A.

claim: TBP is necessary for Mediator transit to promoter regions under conditions of Kin28 depletion.
source: These results, in conjunction with the upstream shift in Mediator occupancy upon depletion of Kin28 and TBP compared to depletion of Kin28 alone (Figure 5), allow us to infer that TBP is necessary for Mediator transit to promoter regions under conditions of Kin28 depletion
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy patterns.

claim: Taf1 association is only slightly decreased upon depletion of TBP by itself or simultaneously with Kin28.
source: In addition, since Taf1 association is only slightly decreased upon depletion of TBP by itself or simultaneously with Kin28 (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Taf1 is not sufficient for Mediator transit from UAS to promoter.
source: we infer that Taf1 is not sufficient for Mediator transit from UAS to promoter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on Taf1 and Mediator occupancy.

claim: Depletion of Rpb3 results in a modest (less than two-fold) reduction in association of both TBP and Taf1.
source: With regard to the role of Taf1 and Pol II in stable occupancy of Mediator at gene promoters (Figure 5), depletion of Rpb3 results in a modest (less than two-fold) reduction in association of both TBP and Taf1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by ChIP-seq data shown in supplementary figures and Figure 7C.

claim: Depletion of Taf1 reduces Pol II occupancy on average about 4-fold, with little difference between SAGA-dominated and TFIID-dominated genes.
source: In contrast, depletion of Taf1 has been shown to reduce Pol II occupancy on average about 4-fold, with little difference between SAGA-dominated and TFIID-dominated genes (Warfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Taf1 by itself appears not to be sufficient to retain Mediator at gene promoters after Kin28 depletion.
source: However, Taf1 (and presumably TFIID) by itself appears not to be sufficient to retain Mediator at gene promoters after Kin28 depletion, as Taf1 is retained when Rpb3 is depleted, while Mediator occupancy is essentially abolished.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on Taf1 and Mediator occupancy.

claim: The partial loss of Pol II accompanying depletion of Taf1 is not sufficient to cause appreciable loss of TBP.
source: Evidently the partial loss of Pol II accompanying depletion of Taf1 is not sufficient to cause appreciable loss of TBP, as no upstream shift in Mediator occupancy was observed upon depletion of Taf1 and Kin28.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy patterns.

claim: Taf1 is not required for recruitment of Mediator to UAS regions.
source: The alternative possibility that Taf1 is required for recruitment of Mediator to UAS regions is ruled out by our observation that Mediator occupancy of UAS regions was not reduced upon depletion of Taf1 alone (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The level of Pol II still associated with gene promoters after Taf1 depletion is sufficient to allow Mediator to stably associate, at least at SAGA-dominated genes.
source: Finally, it appears that the level of Pol II still associated with gene promoters after Taf1 depletion is sufficient to allow Mediator to stably associate, at least at SAGA-dominated genes (compare effects on Med15 occupancy in kin28-rpb3-AA and in kin28-taf1-AA yeast (Figure 5A & C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 5A and C.

claim: TBP is required for transit of Mediator from UAS to gene promoters.
source: In summary, our results indicate that TBP, which is critical for PIC formation, is required for transit of Mediator from UAS to gene promoters
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy patterns after TBP depletion.

claim: Partially formed PICs present after depletion of Taf1 or Rpb3 allow Mediator transit but lead to unstable Mediator-PIC association at promoters.
source: while partially formed PICs present after depletion of Taf1 or Rpb3 allow this transit but lead to unstable Mediator-PIC association at promoters under conditions that prevent the normal rapid turnover of Mediator that accompanies release of Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy after depletion of PIC components.

claim: The Med2-Med3-Med15 tail module triad plays a major role in recruitment of Mediator and Pol II, but is dispensable for viability.
source: The major findings reported in this work are that 1) the Med2-Med3-Med15 tail module triad plays a major role in recruitment of Mediator and Pol II, but is dispensable for viability
evidence: This is a summary of the major findings of the study.

claim: Mediator association with active gene promoters is observed even in the complete absence of the tail module triad.
source: 2) Mediator association with active gene promoters is observed even in the complete absence of the tail module triad
evidence: This is a summary of a major finding of the study.

claim: PIC components, in particular Taf1 and Pol II (Rpb3) contribute to Mediator association with gene promoters, especially at TFIID-dominated genes.
source: 3) PIC components, in particular Taf1 and Pol II (Rpb3) contribute to Mediator association with gene promoters, especially at TFIID-dominated genes
evidence: This is a summary of a major finding of the study.

claim: TBP plays a critical role in the transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter sites.
source: and 4) TBP plays a critical role in the transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter sites.
evidence: This is a summary of a major finding of the study.

claim: Recruitment of Mediator via the tail module triad is likely to occur via activators bound to UAS sites.
source: Recruitment of Mediator via the tail module triad is likely to occur via activators bound to UAS sites, as in the canonical model for gene activation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior models of gene activation.

claim: Mediator is principally recruited first to UAS sites by activators contacting subunits of the tail module triad before transiting to the promoter and facilitating PIC formation.
source: Altogether, then, these various observations support a model in which Mediator is principally recruited first to UAS sites by activators contacting subunits of the tail module triad before transiting to the promoter and facilitating PIC formation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The dominant mechanism of Mediator recruitment is likely to occur via tail-module dependent interactions with UAS-bound activators.
source: Although the dominant mechanism of Mediator recruitment is likely to occur via tail-module dependent interactions with UAS-bound activators
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There exists an alternative, tail-module-independent mechanism for Mediator recruitment.
source: our findings that Mediator and Pol II are recruited to gene promoters even in the complete absence of the tail module triad indicate the existence of an alternative, tail-module-independent mechanism for Mediator recruitment (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Mediator recruitment in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast.

claim: Direct recruitment of Mediator to promoter regions via interactions with PIC components may be favored at TFIID-dominated genes relative to SAGA-dominated genes.
source: Direct recruitment of Mediator to promoter regions via interactions with PIC components may be favored at TFIID-dominated genes relative to SAGA-dominated genes; this would be consistent with the greater effect on Mediator occupancy seen at the former compared to the latter class upon depletion of PIC components (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects observed at different gene classes.

claim: PIC components are important for transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter, and for association with promoters following that transit.
source: Our results indicate that PIC components are important for transit of Mediator from UAS to promoter, and for association with promoters following that transit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy after PIC component depletion.

claim: PIC components are not necessary for recruitment of Mediator to UAS sites.
source: PIC components are not necessary for recruitment of Mediator to UAS sites, as their depletion does not lead to reduction in Mediator association (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Taf1, and presumably TFIID, is important for stabilizing Mediator occupancy at promoters of TFIID-dominated genes following its transit from the initial site of recruitment.
source: Thus, Taf1, and presumably TFIID, is important for stabilizing Mediator occupancy at promoters of TFIID-dominated genes following its transit from the initial site of recruitment
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy after Taf1 depletion.

claim: TBP is critical for the transit from UAS to promoter of both SAGA- and TFIID-dominated genes.
source: whereas TBP is critical for the transit from UAS to promoter of both SAGA- and TFIID-dominated genes (Figure 8, right).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mediator occupancy after TBP depletion.

claim: Cooperative interactions among Mediator, TFIID, and Pol II have been demonstrated in vitro.
source: Related to our findings that PIC components facilitate Mediator association with active gene promoters, in vitro results have indicated cooperative interactions among Mediator, TFIID, and Pol II (Johnson and Carey, 2003; Johnson et al., 2002; Baek et al., 2002; Takahashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Direct recruitment of TFIIB via tethering to the DNA-binding domain of an activator resulted in recruitment of a functional PIC and the Mediator complex in yeast.
source: An 'activator bypass' experiment showed that direct recruitment of TFIIB, via tethering to the DNA-binding domain of an activator, resulted in recruitment of a functional PIC and the Mediator complex in yeast, pointing to 'backwards' recruitment of Mediator via PIC interactions (Lacombe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Depletion of Taf1 results in a widespread reduction in association of head module subunit Med8 with active genes when mapped by ChEC-seq.
source: More recently, depletion of Taf1 was shown to result in a widespread reduction in association of head module subunit Med8 with active genes when mapped by ChEC-seq (Grünberg et al., 2016; Grünberg and Zentner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The head module subcomplexes Med8-Med18-Med20 and Med11-Med17-Med22 bind with TBP.
source: Structural studies have shown the head module subcomplexes Med8-Med18-Med20 and Med11-Med17-Med22 bind with TBP (Cai et al., 2010; Larivière et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Disruption of the Med8-Med18-Med20 subcomplex in med18Δ or med20Δ yeast does not cause loss of viability.
source: Disruption of the Med8-Med18-Med20 subcomplex in med18Δ or med20Δ yeast does not cause loss of viability, suggesting that multiple Mediator-TBP interactions are possible at the proximal promoter for initiation (Ranish et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Interaction between the tail subunits Med15 or Med16 with TFIID subunits Taf14 or Taf1 have been observed in yeast two-hybrid and mass spectrometry experiments.
source: In addition, interaction between the tail subunits Med15 or Med16 with TFIID subunits Taf14 or Taf1 have been observed in yeast two-hybrid and mass spectrometry experiments (Gavin et al., 2006; Gavin et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Interactions between Mediator and Pol II have been demonstrated in both structural and genetic studies.
source: Interactions between Mediator and Pol II have also been demonstrated in both structural and genetic studies (Davis et al., 2002; Esnault et al., 2008; Plaschka et al., 2015; Soutourina et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Interactions between Mediator and Pol II or TFIID appear more important for stabilizing Mediator occupancy at TFIID-dominated genes than for SAGA-dominated genes.
source: Interactions between Mediator and Pol II or TFIID appear more important for stabilizing Mediator occupancy at TFIID-dominated genes than for SAGA-dominated genes, based on the stronger effect on Mediator occupancy in med2∆ med3∆ med15∆ yeast at the latter class than the former (Figure 1), and the stronger effect seen at TFIID-dominated genes upon depletion of Taf1 or Rpb3 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Disruption of a Mediator-TFIIB connection via med10-ts yeast differently reduces association of Mediator, TFIIB, and GTFs at TFIID-dominated versus SAGA-dominated genes.
source: The distinction of these two pathways in terms of dependence on PIC components is also suggested by recent work showing that disruption of a Mediator-TFIIB connection via med10-ts yeast differently reduces association of Mediator, TFIIB, and GTFs (Eychenne et al., 2016). TFIID-dominated genes exhibit a greater reduction in Mediator rather than GTFs, while SAGA-dominated genes exhibit a greater reduction in GTFs rather than Mediator (Eychenne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mediator in general contributes more strongly to Pol II recruitment at SAGA-dominated than TFIID-dominated genes.
source: Furthermore, two recent studies report that Mediator in general, and not just tail module subunits, contributes more strongly to Pol II recruitment at SAGA-dominated than TFIID-dominated genes (Bruzzone et al., 2018; Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The average distance between UAS and TSS is greater for TATA-containing than TATA-less genes.
source: The average distance between UAS and TSS is greater for TATA-containing than TATA-less genes (Kristiansson et al., 2009; Erb and van Nimwegen, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: UASs show diminished ability to activate transcription from a reporter gene as the distance between UAS and TATA box increases.
source: UASs show diminished ability to activate transcription from a reporter gene as the distance between UAS and TATA box increases (Dobi and Winston, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mediator mutations affect the dependence of UAS activity on distance.
source: and Mediator mutations were found to affect the dependence of UAS activity on distance (Reavey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The greater UAS-TSS distance of TATA-containing gene promoters may cause a greater dependency on Mediator for activation.
source: Thus, the greater UAS-TSS distance of TATA-containing gene promoters may cause a greater dependency on Mediator for activation.
